title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Uncertainty-Aware Best-of-N
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be poorly calibrated — they can produce overconfident outputs for incorrect reasoning chains, particularly on out-of-distribution problems or tasks requiring multi-step arithmetic. This miscalibration could cause self-certainty to systematically select wrong-but-confident answers. Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty score with a lightweight calibration layer trained on a small held-out set to map raw self-certainty scores to reliable confidence estimates. We further propose a 'certainty-diversity' composite metric that penalizes candidate sets with low semantic diversity despite high self-certainty, using embedding-based clustering to detect overconfident collapse. No external reward model is required. Experiments: (1) Benchmark self-certainty calibration error (ECE) across GSM8K, MATH, ARC, and TruthfulQA versus CSC; (2) Measure Best-of-N accuracy under distribution shift (train-domain vs. out-of-domain splits); (3) Ablate the certainty-diversity penalty across N={8,16,32,64}; (4) Compare against reward model baselines and vanilla self-certainty on open-ended generation (MT-Bench). We expect CSC to improve Best-of-N selection accuracy by 3-7% on hard out-of-distribution math tasks while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Adaptive Best-of-N via Self-Certainty Thresholding: When to Stop Sampling
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection assumes a fixed N chosen a priori, wasting computation on easy queries that converge quickly while under-sampling hard queries that need more exploration. Self-certainty provides a quality signal, but no work exploits it dynamically to determine when sufficient samples have been collected. Proposed Method: We introduce Certainty-Adaptive Sampling (CAS), which treats self-certainty as a sequential stopping criterion. After each new sample, we compute the running self-certainty score and stop generation when it crosses a learned threshold or when a confidence interval stabilizes (via bootstrap estimation over accumulated samples). The threshold is calibrated per task difficulty using a small held-out validation set, and optionally predicted on-the-fly from prompt embeddings to generalize to unseen tasks. This converts Best-of-N from a static budget into a dynamic compute allocation strategy. Experiments: (1) Compare average N used vs. accuracy against fixed Best-of-N baselines on MATH, GSM8K, and open-ended benchmarks; (2) Plot compute-accuracy Pareto curves showing CAS dominates fixed schedules; (3) Evaluate threshold transfer across task types to test generalization; (4) Compare against speculative decoding and adaptive compute baselines; (5) Analyze how stopping behavior correlates with query difficulty metrics.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Correcting Distributional Bias in LLM Confidence Estimation for Best-of-N Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty leverages LLM output probability distributions as a proxy for response quality, but raw token-level probabilities are known to be poorly calibrated—systematically overconfident or underconfident depending on model size, domain, and generation length. This miscalibration may cause self-certainty scores to favor verbose, repetitive, or stylistically familiar responses over genuinely correct ones, limiting selection quality especially in out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which applies lightweight post-hoc calibration to self-certainty scores. Specifically, we train a small calibration network (e.g., Platt scaling or isotonic regression) on held-out validation sets mapping raw self-certainty scores to empirical accuracy, then use calibrated scores for Best-of-N selection. We additionally propose a length-normalized and domain-adaptive variant that conditions calibration on response length and task type, addressing known length biases in LLM log-probabilities.

Experiments: We evaluate CSC on GSM8K, MATH, ARC-Challenge, and open-ended generation benchmarks (AlpacaEval), comparing against uncalibrated self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model baselines. We measure Expected Calibration Error (ECE), selection accuracy vs. N scaling curves, and cross-domain transfer of calibration parameters. We further analyze failure modes where calibration degrades to characterize when raw self-certainty suffices versus when calibration provides meaningful gains.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in Large Language Models
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be miscalibrated—they can be highly confident yet systematically wrong, particularly on adversarial inputs, out-of-distribution problems, or domains where models exhibit consistent biases. Blindly trusting self-certainty scores may amplify confident errors rather than filtering them.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which combines self-certainty scores with lightweight calibration layers trained to predict actual correctness probability given the raw self-certainty signal and auxiliary features (response length, vocabulary entropy, topic embeddings). Unlike reward models, calibration requires only a small held-out set of labeled examples per domain (~500 samples). We further propose a disagreement-aware fallback: when calibrated confidence is uniformly high but answers diverge structurally, CSC triggers iterative self-refinement rather than selecting the plurality response.

Experiments: (1) Calibration quality measured via ECE across math (MATH-500, GSM8K), coding (HumanEval), and science (MMLU-Pro) benchmarks; (2) Accuracy vs. uncalibrated self-certainty under distribution shift; (3) Adversarial prompt sets where baseline self-certainty fails; (4) Ablation of calibration dataset size; (5) Comparison against reward model selection at matched compute budgets. We expect CSC to expose and correct systematic overconfidence while preserving self-certainty's computational efficiency.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Failures in LLMs
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes that higher distributional confidence correlates with accuracy, but LLMs are known to be miscalibrated — they can exhibit high certainty on incorrect reasoning chains (confidently wrong), particularly on adversarial or out-of-distribution problems. This limits self-certainty's reliability as a selection signal without understanding when it fails.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments self-certainty scores with a calibration layer that detects overconfidence failure modes. First, we train a lightweight calibration head on top of self-certainty scores using held-out data, mapping raw certainty to calibrated correctness probabilities. Second, we propose a diversity-penalized certainty metric that discounts high-certainty selections when sampled responses exhibit low semantic diversity (a signal of degenerate mode collapse). Third, we introduce an uncertainty-triggered fallback mechanism: when calibrated certainty falls below a threshold, CSC escalates to a small verifier model rather than defaulting to potentially overconfident selection.

Experiments: We evaluate on mathematical reasoning (MATH, GSM8K), logical reasoning, and adversarial prompt suites designed to elicit confident failures. We measure Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of selection decisions, accuracy under distribution shift, and cost-accuracy tradeoffs versus full reward models. Ablations isolate each CSC component's contribution.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Diagnosing and Correcting Confidence Miscalibration in Best-of-N Selection
description: Problem: Self-certainty relies on the assumption that LLM output probability distributions are well-calibrated proxies for response quality. However, LLMs are known to exhibit overconfidence or underconfidence depending on domain, model size, and fine-tuning procedure. When self-certainty scores are miscalibrated, Best-of-N selection may systematically favor confidently wrong answers over correct but uncertain ones, degrading performance in specialized or out-of-distribution tasks. Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which applies post-hoc calibration techniques to raw self-certainty scores before Best-of-N selection. Specifically, we (1) collect a small validation set of diverse reasoning problems to estimate the relationship between self-certainty and actual accuracy using temperature scaling and isotonic regression, (2) apply these calibration mappings at inference time to re-rank candidates, and (3) propose a domain-shift-aware variant that clusters responses by topic and performs within-cluster calibration using lightweight embedding-based domain detection. Experiments: We evaluate CSC across math reasoning (MATH, GSM8K), code generation (HumanEval), medical QA (MedQA), and out-of-distribution generalization benchmarks. We measure calibration error (ECE), accuracy improvement over uncalibrated self-certainty, and robustness across model families (Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, Mistral). We also analyze how much calibration data is needed and whether calibration transfers across domains.

title: Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding: When to Stop Sampling in Best-of-N Selection
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection assumes a fixed N determined prior to generation, wasting computation on easy queries where early samples already converge, while potentially under-sampling on genuinely hard problems. Current self-certainty treats N as a static hyperparameter rather than a dynamic stopping criterion. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Self-Certainty (ASC), a sequential sampling framework that monitors the self-certainty score trajectory across accumulated samples and halts generation when a confidence plateau is detected. Specifically, we model the marginal gain in self-certainty as a function of N and fit an online exponential decay estimator; sampling stops when the predicted marginal gain falls below a learned threshold. This threshold is calibrated per difficulty tier using a small validation set, enabling compute-optimal allocation: trivial queries stop at N=2–3, hard queries continue to N=32+. We further propose a 'certainty volatility' signal—variance of self-certainty across recent samples—as an additional stopping feature to detect oscillating, genuinely ambiguous problems. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended creative tasks (AlpacaEval) measuring accuracy vs. average samples used. Baselines include fixed-N self-certainty, reward model selection, and speculative early-exit methods. We expect 30–50% reduction in average N with <1% accuracy loss, demonstrating compute-optimal test-time scaling.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Failure Modes in LLM Test-Time Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can exhibit systematic overconfidence — producing high-certainty wrong answers, particularly on adversarial inputs, out-of-distribution problems, or domains where models have memorized incorrect patterns. This miscalibration could make self-certainty-based Best-of-N selection worse than random in specific failure regimes.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which learns a lightweight post-hoc calibration layer that maps raw self-certainty scores to calibrated confidence estimates. Specifically, we (1) collect a held-out calibration dataset pairing self-certainty scores with binary correctness labels across diverse task types, (2) fit a temperature-scaled isotonic regression model per domain, and (3) incorporate uncertainty about the calibration itself via conformal prediction intervals. When calibrated confidence falls below a threshold, CSC falls back to a diversity-promoting selection strategy rather than pure argmax, explicitly trading off certainty for response diversity.

Experiments: We evaluate on standard math/reasoning benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, MMLU) plus adversarial variants (misleading premises, counterfactual questions). We measure calibration error (ECE), selective accuracy curves, and Best-of-N accuracy vs. N scaling. Ablations compare uncalibrated self-certainty, temperature scaling alone, and full CSC, with analysis of failure mode categories where overconfidence is most prevalent.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Chains via Uncertainty Decomposition
description:
Problem: Self-certainty aggregates token-level probability distributions to estimate response quality, but LLMs are known to be miscalibrated — they can exhibit high distributional certainty on confidently wrong reasoning chains (epistemic overconfidence). This creates a failure mode where self-certainty selects high-confidence but incorrect responses, particularly on knowledge-intensive or multi-step mathematical reasoning tasks where models may hallucinate plausible-sounding but false intermediate steps.

Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into two components: (1) aleatoric uncertainty, capturing genuine ambiguity in the task, and (2) epistemic uncertainty, reflecting model knowledge gaps. We estimate epistemic uncertainty by measuring disagreement in self-certainty scores across semantically distinct response clusters (building on universal self-consistency clustering). We then apply a calibration correction — penalizing responses where high self-certainty conflicts with high inter-cluster epistemic uncertainty — producing 'calibrated self-certainty' (CSC). When epistemic uncertainty is high, CSC triggers a targeted self-refinement step using uncertainty-aware prompting.

Experiments: Evaluate on MATH-500, GPQA, MedQA, and HotpotQA across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and GPT-4o-mini. Compare against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model baselines. Measure accuracy vs. N scaling, calibration (ECE), and failure-mode reduction on overconfident-wrong cases specifically.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Identifying and Correcting Overconfident Failures in LLM Best-of-N Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on certain problem types (e.g., multi-step arithmetic, counterfactual reasoning), leading Best-of-N selection to confidently pick wrong answers. This failure mode is underexplored and limits reliability in high-stakes applications.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which combines self-certainty scores with a lightweight calibration layer trained to detect domain-specific overconfidence patterns. Specifically, we (1) characterize when self-certainty miscalibrates by analyzing disagreement between self-certainty rankings and ground truth across problem taxonomies; (2) train a small auxiliary classifier on features derived from token-level entropy distributions and semantic clustering of candidate responses to predict miscalibration likelihood; (3) when miscalibration risk is high, fall back to a diversity-weighted selection strategy that penalizes over-represented answer clusters.

Experiments: We evaluate CSC on MATH-500, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, and a new adversarial benchmark of deliberately confounding problems across N∈{4,8,16,32}. Metrics include selection accuracy, calibration ECE of the certainty scores, and compute overhead vs. reward model baselines. We analyze failure mode reduction and compare against vanilla self-certainty, universal self-consistency, and ORM-based selection.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Failures in LLM Test-Time Selection
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on certain problem types (e.g., multi-step arithmetic, counterfactual reasoning), producing high self-certainty scores for wrong answers. Third, we propose a temperature-adaptive sampling scheme that dynamically adjusts generation temperature based on detected calibration quality. We measure calibration (ECE), accuracy@N curves, and compare against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model baselines across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and Mistral model families.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Best-of-N Selection in Long-Horizon Reasoning
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes that higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on specific failure modes—particularly in multi-step mathematical proofs, code generation with subtle bugs, and factual reasoning where plausible-sounding errors cluster together. This miscalibration may cause self-certainty to consistently select wrong-but-confident answers over correct-but-uncertain ones, especially in long-horizon tasks where early errors propagate. Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty score with a step-level uncertainty decomposition. Rather than aggregating token probabilities across entire responses, CSC segments responses into reasoning steps, computes per-step certainty, and applies isotonic regression calibration learned from a small held-out set to correct systematic overconfidence patterns. We additionally propose a diversity-aware reranking mechanism that penalizes clusters of near-identical high-certainty responses, forcing selection among more diverse candidates when overconfidence is detected. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH-500, GSM8K, HumanEval+, GPQA, and a new long-chain proof benchmark across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and DeepSeek-R1 models. We measure calibration error (ECE) of selection decisions, accuracy vs. N scaling curves, and compare against vanilla self-certainty, process reward models, and Monte Carlo Tree Search baselines, demonstrating improved reliability on tasks where standard self-certainty degrades.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Distribution-Aware Temperature Scaling
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can exhibit systematic overconfidence—generating highly certain but wrong responses—particularly in domains with distribution shift or adversarial inputs. This miscalibration undermines Best-of-N selection reliability and may cause confident selection of incorrect reasoning chains.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty metric with post-hoc calibration. Specifically, we (1) train a lightweight calibration head on held-out data that maps raw self-certainty scores to calibrated confidence estimates, accounting for task type, response length, and token-level uncertainty patterns; (2) apply distribution-aware temperature scaling per reasoning domain rather than globally; and (3) introduce a 'certainty-accuracy gap' detector that flags overconfident-but-wrong responses by comparing self-certainty against a diversity penalty measuring semantic spread across N samples.

Experiments: We evaluate CSC on MATH, GSM8K, MedQA, and out-of-distribution benchmarks (ARC-Challenge variants with rephrased distractors). We measure Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of Best-of-N selection, accuracy under distribution shift, and compare against uncalibrated self-certainty, reward models, and ensemble methods. Ablations isolate contribution of each calibration component. We hypothesize CSC reduces overconfident failures by 25%+ while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Correcting Distribution Shift Bias in Token-Probability-Based Best-of-N Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty relies on aggregated token log-probabilities to estimate response quality, but these probabilities are systematically miscalibrated due to factors like temperature scaling, model size, and instruction-tuning RLHF alignment shifts. This miscalibration means raw self-certainty scores may be biased toward shorter responses, simpler vocabulary, or in-distribution phrasings rather than genuinely better reasoning—limiting reliability across diverse tasks and models.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which corrects for known distributional biases in LLM output probabilities before aggregation. Specifically, we apply three corrections: (1) length normalization with a learned exponent rather than a fixed one, (2) vocabulary-frequency debiasing that downweights probability mass on high-frequency tokens that dominate log-probability sums, and (3) a lightweight isotonic regression calibrator trained on a small held-out validation set to map raw self-certainty scores to accuracy-predictive confidence estimates. The calibrator requires only ~500 examples and no reward model supervision.

Experiments: We evaluate CSC against vanilla self-certainty, universal self-consistency, and reward-model-based selection on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended writing tasks (MT-Bench) across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and Mistral model families. We measure Best-of-N accuracy curves, calibration error (ECE), and performance versus N scaling behavior, demonstrating that bias correction yields consistent improvements, especially for smaller N and harder problems.

title: Adaptive N-Selection: Dynamically Allocating Test-Time Compute via Self-Certainty Thresholds
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection treats N as a fixed hyperparameter, wastefully applying the same computational budget to both trivial and hard queries. Ideally, a system should generate few samples for easy questions and many for hard ones—but without a reward model, knowing when to stop is non-trivial. Proposed Method: We leverage self-certainty as an online stopping criterion. After each new sample, we compute the running self-certainty score; if it exceeds a learned or heuristically-set confidence threshold, generation halts early. We frame this as an adaptive compute allocation problem and explore three threshold strategies: (1) fixed global thresholds tuned on a validation set, (2) query-complexity-conditioned thresholds estimated from prompt perplexity, and (3) a lightweight meta-predictor trained to predict required N from prompt features. We also introduce a 'certainty saturation' metric to detect when additional samples yield diminishing returns. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended generation benchmarks (AlpacaEval), measuring accuracy-vs-FLOPs Pareto curves against fixed-N baselines and reward-model-based adaptive methods. We hypothesize adaptive self-certainty achieves 80%+ of maximum-N accuracy while reducing average sample count by 40-60%, yielding a superior efficiency-accuracy tradeoff across difficulty strata.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Best-of-N: Combining Self-Certainty with Epistemic Calibration for Reliable LLM Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty aggregates distributional confidence across samples to select the best response, but conflates aleatoric uncertainty (inherent task ambiguity) with epistemic uncertainty (model knowledge gaps). A high self-certainty score on an unfamiliar problem may indicate overconfident hallucination rather than genuine correctness, limiting reliability in high-stakes domains like medical reasoning or legal analysis.

Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into aleatoric and epistemic components using ensemble-based token probability disagreement across model variants (e.g., different temperatures, LoRA-finetuned checkpoints, or quantization levels). We define 'calibrated self-certainty' as self-certainty weighted by epistemic confidence, penalizing selections where model variants disagree on the probability distribution despite high individual certainty. When epistemic uncertainty exceeds a threshold, the system falls back to a lightweight verifier or abstains.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate calibrated self-certainty vs. baseline self-certainty on MMLU-Pro, MedQA, and LegalBench across Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 models. (2) Measure selective prediction performance (accuracy-abstention tradeoffs). (3) Analyze correlation between epistemic uncertainty estimates and actual error rates. (4) Test scaling behavior with N samples under distribution shift. (5) Compare computational overhead against reward model baselines. We hypothesize calibrated self-certainty yields better ECE and AUROC on error detection with minimal added cost.

title: Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding: Early Stopping for Efficient Best-of-N Inference
description:
Problem: Best-of-N selection with self-certainty still requires generating all N samples before selecting the best response, wasting computation when early samples already exhibit high confidence. Current methods lack principled stopping criteria that balance quality and efficiency dynamically.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding (ASCT), a sequential inference framework that monitors the self-certainty score as samples are generated one-by-one and terminates sampling early when certainty surpasses a learned or analytically-derived confidence threshold. We model the problem as a sequential hypothesis test: given accumulated self-certainty after k samples, decide whether to commit to the current best response or draw another sample. We explore two variants: (1) a fixed-threshold variant derived from calibration data, and (2) a meta-learned threshold conditioned on task difficulty signals (prompt perplexity, token count) using a lightweight MLP trained on held-out examples.

Experiments: We evaluate on GSM8K, MATH, ARC-Challenge, and open-ended generation benchmarks (AlpacaEval). We measure average samples-to-decision vs. accuracy tradeoff curves, comparing against uniform Best-of-N with self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model baselines. Key metrics include accuracy-at-compute-budget and average N used per query, demonstrating that ASCT achieves comparable accuracy to Best-of-16 with average effective N closer to 4-6 on easy problems while preserving quality on hard ones.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Sampling: Dynamic N Selection via Self-Certainty Convergence Detection
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection methods typically require fixing N in advance, leading to wasted computation on easy queries (where N=4 suffices) and insufficient exploration on hard ones (where N=64 is needed). Self-certainty provides a principled signal for response quality, but its potential for dynamic, query-adaptive compute allocation remains unexplored. Method: We propose Self-Certainty Convergence Detection (SCCD), an online stopping criterion that monitors the trajectory of self-certainty scores as samples are drawn sequentially. Specifically, we compute a running self-certainty estimate after each new sample and stop sampling when the estimate stabilizes within a threshold (measured via variance over a sliding window). This transforms Best-of-N into adaptive Best-of-N*, where N* is query-dependent. We additionally introduce a difficulty-aware temperature scheduler that increases sampling temperature when self-certainty plateaus at low values, encouraging diversity on hard problems. Experiments: We evaluate SCCD on MATH, GSM8K, GPQA, and open-ended generation benchmarks (AlpacaEval), measuring (1) average N* versus fixed-N baselines at matched accuracy, (2) compute-accuracy Pareto curves, (3) correlation between early self-certainty trajectories and final answer correctness, and (4) comparison against Speculative Decoding and reward-model-gated early exit methods. We expect 30-50% average compute reduction at matched performance.

(3) Measure Expected Calibration Error of raw vs. calibrated scores. (4) Ablate contrastive certainty contribution. (5) Test whether CSC closes the gap with reward-model-based selection on hard problems where raw self-certainty fails.

title: Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding: Early Exit and Selective Sampling for Efficient Test-Time Computation
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection with self-certainty improves reasoning quality but still requires generating all N samples before selection, wasting computation when high-certainty consensus emerges early. Current approaches treat N as a fixed hyperparameter rather than adapting dynamically to problem difficulty and emerging confidence signals. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Self-Certainty (ASC), a sequential sampling framework that monitors self-certainty scores incrementally after each new sample and applies learned stopping criteria. Specifically, we train a lightweight meta-predictor that observes the running self-certainty trajectory (certainty value, variance across samples, rate of change) and predicts whether additional samples will change the selected answer. We combine this with difficulty-aware initialization: using a fast proxy model to estimate problem difficulty and set minimum sample budgets accordingly. For open-ended tasks, we extend self-certainty with semantic clustering to enable meaningful early-exit signals. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended benchmarks (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and DeepSeek-R1 model families. We measure accuracy-vs-compute Pareto frontiers comparing fixed-N self-certainty, reward models, and ASC. We demonstrate that ASC achieves comparable accuracy to N=32 while using on average 40-60% fewer samples, with largest gains on easy problems where certainty converges quickly.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Failure Modes in LLM Test-Time Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be overconfident on certain failure modes—e.g., consistently wrong reasoning chains, sycophantic patterns, or domain-specific blind spots. When a model generates N samples that are uniformly wrong but highly self-certain, Best-of-N selection will confidently select an incorrect answer, creating a systematic failure mode worse than random selection.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty score with an uncertainty-of-uncertainty estimate. Specifically, we (1) compute per-token entropy variance across the N samples to detect pathological low-diversity regimes, (2) apply a diversity penalty that discounts self-certainty scores when the N samples cluster too tightly in token-probability space, and (3) train a lightweight probe (using only model internals—no external reward model) to predict miscalibration likelihood from self-certainty distribution statistics. When miscalibration is detected, CSC falls back to increased temperature sampling to escape the overconfidence trap.

Experiments: Evaluate on standard reasoning benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, MMLU) but focus on adversarially constructed subsets where baseline self-certainty fails. Compare against self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward-model-based selection. Measure calibration (ECE), accuracy, and failure mode frequency as N scales from 4 to 64.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Debiasing Token Probability Aggregation for Reliable Best-of-N Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty leverages LLM output probability distributions to score candidate responses, but raw token log-probabilities are systematically biased by factors including response length, vocabulary frequency artifacts, and model-specific probability calibration errors. These biases cause self-certainty scores to favor shorter, higher-frequency-token responses even when longer, more accurate responses exist, limiting its reliability especially on tasks requiring detailed multi-step answers.

Proposed Method: We propose Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which debiases self-certainty scores through three complementary corrections: (1) length-normalized log-probability aggregation with learned length penalty coefficients estimated from held-out data, (2) vocabulary-level frequency correction by subtracting token-wise unigram baseline log-probabilities, and (3) temperature-aware ensemble aggregation that weights samples by their distributional spread rather than treating all N samples equally. The calibration parameters are estimated efficiently using a small reference set without requiring labeled examples.

Experiments: We evaluate CSC on MATH, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, and open-ended generation benchmarks (AlpacaEval, MT-Bench) across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and Mistral model families. We compare against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, universal self-consistency, and reward model baselines across varying N (1-64). We specifically analyze performance stratified by response length and task complexity, and measure calibration quality via Expected Calibration Error of the selection scores against ground-truth accuracy.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Identifying and Correcting Systematic Overconfidence in LLM Test-Time Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes that higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be miscalibrated—exhibiting systematic overconfidence on specific problem types (e.g., multi-step arithmetic, counterfactual reasoning) or for certain demographic phrasings. When self-certainty is miscalibrated, Best-of-N selection may consistently promote confidently wrong answers, undermining the approach's reliability at scale.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which learns a lightweight post-hoc recalibration mapping from raw self-certainty scores to calibrated confidence estimates. Using a small held-out calibration set per domain, we fit isotonic regression or temperature scaling on (self-certainty score, correctness) pairs. We further propose a difficulty-aware reweighting scheme that downweights self-certainty for problem categories where overconfidence is empirically detected, using a classifier trained to identify such categories from question features alone—requiring no ground-truth labels at inference time.

Experiments: (1) Calibration analysis across GSM8K, MATH, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge, measuring ECE before/after calibration. (2) Best-of-N accuracy with CSC vs. vanilla self-certainty and reward models at N={4,8,16,32,64}. (3) Transfer of calibration across related domains. (4) Ablations on calibration set size and difficulty-aware reweighting. We expect CSC to reduce overconfidence failures while maintaining scalability advantages.

title: Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding: Early Exit Strategies for Efficient Best-of-N Selection
description: Problem: Self-certainty improves Best-of-N selection without reward models, but still requires generating all N samples before selection, wasting computation when high-certainty responses emerge early. We propose Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding (ASCT), a dynamic early-exit framework that monitors self-certainty scores incrementally as samples are generated and terminates sampling once sufficient confidence is reached, reducing average computation while maintaining quality. Method: We formulate early stopping as a sequential decision problem. After each new sample, we update a running self-certainty estimate and compare against a learned confidence threshold. The threshold is calibrated per-task using a small held-out set, balancing accuracy preservation against compute savings. We additionally propose a variance-aware stopping criterion that accounts for self-certainty stability across successive samples, preventing premature termination in ambiguous cases. We also explore combining ASCT with speculative decoding to further amortize costs. Experiments: We evaluate on mathematical reasoning (MATH, GSM8K), code generation (HumanEval, MBPP), and open-ended QA (TriviaQA, ARC-Challenge) across Llama-3, Mistral, and Qwen-2.5 model families. We measure accuracy vs. average samples generated trade-offs, comparing against fixed-N self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward-model baselines. Expected result: ASCT achieves 40-60% reduction in average samples generated with less than 1% accuracy degradation relative to full Best-of-N self-certainty.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Uncertainty-Aware Best-of-N Selection
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be miscalibrated — they can be highly certain about wrong answers, especially on out-of-distribution or adversarial reasoning problems. This systematic overconfidence undermines self-certainty's reliability as a selection signal. Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty score with a calibration correction layer. Specifically, we (1) estimate a per-domain confidence-accuracy calibration curve using a small held-out validation set, (2) apply isotonic regression to transform raw self-certainty scores into calibrated probability estimates, and (3) incorporate an epistemic uncertainty penalty derived from the variance of token-level log-probabilities across N samples to down-weight spuriously confident but inconsistent responses. When calibrated certainty is low across all candidates, CSC triggers a fallback to semantic clustering (universal self-consistency) to prevent overconfident wrong selections. Experiments: We evaluate CSC on standard reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ARC), adversarial reasoning datasets (TruthfulQA, MMLU hard splits), and out-of-distribution tasks. We measure selection accuracy, Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and performance at varying N. Ablations isolate contributions of isotonic calibration versus epistemic penalty. We compare against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and lightweight reward models across Llama-3, Mistral, and Qwen-2.5 model families.

title: Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding: Early Stopping in Best-of-N Sampling via Confidence Saturation Detection
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection with self-certainty still requires pre-specifying N upfront, wasting computation on easy queries that saturate quickly while potentially under-sampling hard queries that need more candidates. This fixed-N regime is fundamentally inefficient across heterogeneous query difficulties. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Self-Certainty (ASC), a dynamic stopping criterion that monitors the running self-certainty score as samples are drawn sequentially, halting generation when the score's marginal gain falls below a learned difficulty-conditioned threshold. Specifically, we model self-certainty accumulation as a saturation curve, fitting a lightweight exponential smoothing estimator online. A small meta-classifier trained on query features (prompt perplexity, token entropy) predicts an instance-specific saturation tolerance, enabling easy queries to terminate at N=2–3 while hard queries continue to N=32+. This requires no reward model and adds negligible overhead. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended generation (AlpacaEval) comparing: (1) fixed-N self-certainty, (2) fixed-N reward model selection, and (3) ASC. Primary metrics include accuracy-per-FLOP curves, average effective N, and correlation between predicted difficulty and actual stopping point. We expect ASC to match fixed N=16 accuracy while using average N≈5, demonstrating substantial compute savings across difficulty distributions.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Distributional Uncertainty Decomposition
description: Problem: Self-certainty relies on aggregated output probability distributions to select the best response, but high distributional certainty can arise from two distinct sources: genuine model competence (epistemic certainty) or systematic overconfidence in wrong answers (miscalibration). When a model is consistently wrong with high confidence—common in domain-shifted or adversarial reasoning tasks—self-certainty selects the most confidently wrong answer, actively harming performance. Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into aleatoric uncertainty (inherent task ambiguity) and epistemic uncertainty (model knowledge gaps) using an ensemble-free approach: we apply targeted token-level perturbations (synonym substitutions, paraphrase variants) to generated responses and measure consistency of probability distributions across perturbed variants. Responses with high aggregate certainty but high sensitivity to perturbations signal miscalibrated overconfidence. We introduce a corrected selection metric, Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), that discounts responses exhibiting this pattern and optionally triggers a fallback to diversity-promoting sampling strategies. Experiments: We evaluate CSC on (1) standard benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, MMLU) where self-certainty performs well as a baseline, (2) out-of-distribution reasoning tasks where models are known to be overconfident, (3) adversarially constructed problems with plausible but systematically wrong high-confidence attractors, and (4) scaling analysis across N=1 to N=64 samples on multiple model families. We expect CSC to match self-certainty on in-distribution tasks while substantially outperforming it in overconfidence-prone settings.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Distribution-Aware Temperature Scaling
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes that higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be miscalibrated — they can produce high-certainty outputs for confidently wrong answers, particularly in domains requiring multi-step arithmetic, counterfactual reasoning, or knowledge-intensive tasks. This miscalibration fundamentally limits the reliability of self-certainty as a Best-of-N selector.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which learns a lightweight, domain-adaptive calibration layer on top of raw self-certainty scores. Specifically, we (1) collect self-certainty scores alongside ground-truth correctness labels across diverse reasoning tasks to characterize miscalibration patterns, (2) apply temperature scaling and isotonic regression post-hoc to map raw certainty scores to calibrated confidence estimates, and (3) propose a dynamic threshold mechanism that adjusts selection criteria based on detected task type and uncertainty regime. Crucially, CSC requires no external reward model and adds negligible computation overhead.

Experiments: We evaluate CSC on GSM8K, MATH, StrategyQA, TruthfulQA, and open-ended generation benchmarks. Metrics include Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Best-of-N accuracy curves, and correlation between certainty scores and correctness. We compare against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward-model baselines, ablating calibration methods and temperature choices across multiple LLM families (Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, Mistral).

title: Adaptive Best-of-N via Dynamic Self-Certainty Thresholds: Knowing When to Stop Sampling
description:
Problem: Best-of-N selection with self-certainty still requires fixing N in advance, leading to wasted computation on easy queries (where N=2 suffices) and insufficient exploration on hard ones (where N=100 may still underperform). An adaptive stopping criterion that dynamically determines when enough samples have been drawn would substantially improve compute efficiency.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Self-Certainty Sampling (ASCS), which treats self-certainty as an online signal to implement an early-stopping policy during inference. After each new sample, we compute a running self-certainty estimate and compare it against a learned or calibrated confidence threshold. If certainty exceeds the threshold, sampling halts; otherwise it continues up to a maximum budget N_max. We additionally propose a difficulty-aware threshold that is conditioned on query complexity features (estimated via a lightweight classifier or initial token probabilities), allowing tighter budgets on simple queries and relaxed ones on harder instances.

Experiments: (1) Compare compute-accuracy tradeoff curves (FLOPs vs. accuracy) against fixed-N self-certainty, reward models, and self-consistency across MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended instruction-following benchmarks. (2) Analyze stopping-point distributions across difficulty strata. (3) Evaluate calibration of the adaptive threshold via expected calibration error. (4) Test generalization to code generation (HumanEval+). We expect ASCS to match fixed-N top performance at 40-60% of the average compute cost.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Chains via Uncertainty-Aware Best-of-N Selection
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on specific reasoning failure modes (e.g., arithmetic errors, faulty logical steps mid-chain). A high aggregate self-certainty score may mask localized uncertainty spikes within a chain, selecting confidently wrong answers over cautiously correct ones. Method: We propose Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which computes token-level self-certainty profiles across sampled chains rather than a single aggregate score. CSC identifies 'uncertainty breakpoints'—positions where confidence drops sharply within otherwise high-certainty chains—and uses these profiles for two purposes: (1) a refined Best-of-N selector that penalizes chains with high aggregate certainty but large variance in local certainty (flagging brittle reasoning), and (2) a targeted revision step that regenerates only the low-certainty spans using constrained decoding conditioned on surrounding high-certainty context. Experiments: We evaluate CSC on GSM8K, MATH, ARC-Challenge, and medical reasoning benchmarks (MedQA), comparing against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model baselines. We further analyze calibration via Expected Calibration Error before/after CSC, and measure compute-accuracy trade-offs as N scales. Ablations isolate the contribution of breakpoint penalization versus span-level revision.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Best-of-N Selection via Distribution Shift Awareness
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes that high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on certain problem types (e.g., multi-step arithmetic, counterfactual reasoning, out-of-distribution prompts). This miscalibration causes self-certainty to confidently select wrong answers, undermining its reliability precisely when it matters most. Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty score with a lightweight distribution-shift detector. For each query, we estimate whether the prompt lies in a region where self-certainty is historically miscalibrated by (1) computing a per-instance uncertainty-accuracy calibration score using a small held-out probe set, (2) training a cheap regression head on top of frozen LLM embeddings to predict self-certainty miscalibration as a function of input features, and (3) dynamically reweighting or falling back to diversity-based selection (universal self-consistency) when predicted miscalibration exceeds a threshold. Planned Experiments: We evaluate CSC on GSM8K, MATH, StrategyQA, and TruthfulQA across Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 model families, measuring calibration curves (ECE), selection accuracy at varying N (4,8,16,32,64), and performance on adversarially constructed overconfidence-inducing prompts. We compare against vanilla self-certainty, reward models, and self-consistency baselines, demonstrating improved reliability without added inference cost.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Identifying and Correcting Systematic Overconfidence in LLM Test-Time Selection
description: Problem: Self-certainty leverages token probability distributions to score Best-of-N candidates, but LLMs are known to be poorly calibrated — systematically overconfident or underconfident in ways that vary across domains, model sizes, and reasoning types. Uncalibrated self-certainty scores may systematically favor certain response styles (e.g., shorter, more formulaic answers) regardless of correctness, limiting reliability as N scales. Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which learns a lightweight post-hoc calibration layer that maps raw self-certainty scores to calibrated selection probabilities. Calibration is performed using a small held-out set of (prompt, response, correctness) triples via temperature scaling and isotonic regression variants adapted for the distributional aggregation structure of self-certainty. We further propose a domain-adaptive variant that clusters prompts by estimated difficulty and applies cluster-specific calibration. Crucially, calibration requires no reward model — only LLM-generated samples and self-evaluated correctness signals via consistency checks. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, HotpotQA, and open-ended writing tasks across Llama-3, Mistral, and Qwen model families. Metrics include Best-of-N accuracy, Expected Calibration Error of selection scores, and performance under distribution shift. We compare against uncalibrated self-certainty, universal self-consistency, and reward model baselines, demonstrating that calibration meaningfully improves selection quality especially at small N where raw self-certainty is noisiest.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Failure Modes in LLM Test-Time Scaling
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can exhibit systematic overconfidence on specific failure modes—hallucinations, spurious reasoning shortcuts, or domain-shifted inputs—where the model confidently generates wrong answers across multiple samples. This creates a critical blind spot: Best-of-N selection via self-certainty may consistently select high-confidence wrong answers, performing worse than random selection in adversarial or out-of-distribution settings.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which combines self-certainty scores with lightweight epistemic uncertainty estimation to detect overconfident failure modes. CSC computes a diversity-weighted certainty score that penalizes cases where high self-certainty coincides with low semantic diversity across N samples—a signal that the model has collapsed to a confident but potentially wrong attractor. When this collapse is detected, CSC triggers a fallback strategy: either resampling with elevated temperature or escalating to a small verifier model only for flagged responses.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) standard reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU), (2) adversarial variants with misleading premises, (3) out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning, and (4) factual QA with known LLM hallucination patterns. We compare CSC against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model selection, measuring accuracy, calibration error, and compute efficiency across N=1 to N=64 samples.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Best-of-N Selection via Uncertainty-Aware Ensemble Reranking
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes that higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be poorly calibrated—they can produce overconfident yet wrong responses, especially on out-of-distribution or adversarial inputs. This miscalibration could cause self-certainty-based Best-of-N to systematically select confidently wrong answers, a critical failure mode for high-stakes applications.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments self-certainty scores with a lightweight calibration layer trained on held-out validation data. CSC estimates not just the raw self-certainty score but also its reliability by modeling the conditional probability P(correct | self-certainty score, task-type, input difficulty). We further propose a hybrid reranker that interpolates between self-certainty and semantic diversity signals: when calibrated confidence is low, diversity-weighted voting is upweighted to hedge against overconfident clusters. No external reward model is needed.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark CSC against vanilla self-certainty on standard reasoning tasks (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU) plus adversarial perturbation variants. (2) Evaluate calibration metrics (ECE, reliability diagrams) across N=1 to 64 samples. (3) Test on medical QA and legal reasoning as high-stakes domains. (4) Ablate the interpolation weighting scheme to quantify when diversity vs. certainty dominates. We expect CSC to maintain Best-of-N scaling benefits while substantially reducing overconfident selection errors.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Chains via Distributional Uncertainty Decomposition
description:
Problem: Self-certainty aggregates token-level probability distributions to estimate response quality, but high distributional certainty can reflect confidently wrong reasoning — a known failure mode where LLMs are overconfident on systematic errors or hallucinations. This misalignment between certainty and correctness limits reliability in high-stakes domains like medical reasoning or legal analysis.

Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into two components: (1) aleatoric uncertainty, capturing inherent ambiguity in the problem, and (2) epistemic uncertainty, reflecting model knowledge gaps. We operationalize this via a lightweight auxiliary calibration head trained on top of frozen LLM hidden states using a small labeled calibration set (~500 examples), mapping raw self-certainty scores to calibrated quality estimates. We further introduce a 'certainty-consistency gap' metric: when high self-certainty and low self-consistency co-occur, we trigger targeted re-sampling with modified decoding parameters to escape local probability modes.

Experiments: Evaluate on MATH, MedQA, LegalBench, and TruthfulQA. Compare against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model baselines on accuracy, calibration (ECE), and abstention quality. Ablate calibration set size, decomposition method, and re-sampling trigger thresholds. Demonstrate that calibrated self-certainty achieves better accuracy-confidence alignment with minimal computational overhead over standard self-certainty.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Failures in LLM Best-of-N Selection
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be miscalibrated — they can exhibit high self-certainty on confidently wrong answers (hallucinations), particularly in knowledge-intensive or ambiguous domains. This creates a systematic failure mode where Best-of-N selection amplifies errors rather than filtering them. Second, we introduce a 'certainty-diversity' trade-off metric that penalizes low response diversity alongside high certainty, flagging potentially overconfident collapse. Third, we propose a hybrid selection strategy that falls back to semantic clustering (à la universal self-consistency) when calibrated certainty exceeds a suspicion threshold. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) medical QA (MedQA, PubMedQA) where hallucination is costly, (2) ambiguous commonsense benchmarks (WinoGrande), (3) mathematical reasoning (MATH), measuring both accuracy and ECE (expected calibration error) of selection decisions across N=1 to N=64, comparing against vanilla self-certainty, reward models, and self-consistency baselines.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Failures in LLMs
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can exhibit systematic overconfidence on certain problem types (e.g., misleading math word problems, counterfactual reasoning, adversarial prompts), where high self-certainty actually signals confidently wrong answers. When calibrated confidence falls below a learned threshold despite high raw self-certainty, CSC triggers a 'disagreement-seeking' fallback: it actively re-samples with increased temperature and entropy-promoting prompts to escape overconfident failure modes. Experiments: (1) Benchmark on standard reasoning tasks (GSM8K, MATH, ARC) measuring calibration ECE alongside accuracy; (2) Adversarial reasoning datasets where vanilla self-certainty fails; (3) Ablations comparing CSC thresholding strategies; (4) Scaling analysis of calibration sample requirements; (5) Comparison against reward-model-based selection on calibration metrics. title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Best-of-N Selection via Uncertainty-Aware Reranking
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs are known to be poorly calibrated—they can be confidently wrong. This miscalibration may cause self-certainty to systematically favor plausible-sounding but incorrect responses, particularly on novel or out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Current work lacks analysis of when and why self-certainty fails due to overconfidence. Specifically, we (1) compute self-certainty scores across N samples, (2) estimate a 'diversity-confidence tension' signal measuring disagreement between high-certainty candidates, and (3) apply a learned isotonic regression calibrator that adjusts certainty scores based on task-type embeddings and response diversity statistics. When overconfidence is detected, CSC falls back to a diversity-weighted ensemble combining self-certainty with semantic spread metrics. Experiments: We evaluate on standard math/reasoning benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, ARC), adversarial reasoning sets designed to elicit confident errors, code generation (HumanEval), and ambiguous open-ended QA. title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in Large Language Models

Key analyses include: calibration curves before/after correction, ECE metrics, performance under distribution shift, and scaling behavior with N. title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Best-of-N Selection via Uncertainty-Aware Ensemble Scoring
description:

This miscalibration undermines reliable Best-of-N selection at scale.

Rather than using self-certainty as a direct ranking metric, we fit a temperature-scaling + feature-augmented calibrator that takes as input: (1) raw self-certainty score, (2) pairwise response similarity variance across the N samples, (3) response length statistics, and (4) estimated epistemic uncertainty via Monte Carlo dropout over the scoring pass. The calibrator produces reliability-adjusted scores enabling better discrimination between confidently-correct and confidently-wrong responses.

Experiments: (1) Calibration curves (ECE) comparing raw vs. calibrated self-certainty on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended summarization; (2) Best-of-N accuracy across N={4,8,16,32,64} vs. reward model baselines; (3) OOD robustness tests using domain-shifted datasets; (4) Ablation over calibration features; (5) Analysis of overconfidence failure modes.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Distributional Uncertainty Decomposition
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on specific failure modes (e.g., mathematical errors, factual hallucinations), making raw self-certainty scores misleading. A model may generate N highly consistent but collectively wrong responses, causing Best-of-N to confidently select incorrect answers.

Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into two components: (1) aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible ambiguity in the question) and (2) epistemic uncertainty (model knowledge gaps). We estimate aleatoric uncertainty via token-level entropy variance across semantically equivalent question paraphrases, and epistemic uncertainty via distributional divergence between self-certainty scores computed on the original versus perturbed prompts. A calibrated selection score combines these components, penalizing high-certainty clusters that exhibit fragility to prompt perturbation—a signal of overconfident hallucination rather than genuine knowledge.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on MATH, GSM8K, TruthfulQA, and MMLU comparing calibrated vs. raw self-certainty and reward model baselines; (2) Ablation on perturbation strategies (paraphrase, few-shot reordering, template variation); (3) Analysis of overconfidence failure modes across model families (Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, Mistral); (4) Scaling curves showing improved precision-recall tradeoff at high N. We expect 3-7% accuracy gains on hard mathematical subsets where standard self-certainty degrades.

title: Adaptive Sample Allocation via Self-Certainty: Spending Test-Time Compute Where It Matters
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection treats all queries uniformly, allocating the same N samples regardless of problem difficulty. This wastes compute on easy questions while under-sampling hard ones, limiting the efficiency of test-time scaling. Proposed Method: We introduce Self-Certainty Guided Adaptive Sampling (SCGAS), which uses self-certainty scores as an online difficulty signal to dynamically allocate a variable number of samples per query within a fixed total compute budget. Starting with a small initial batch (e.g., N=4), SCGAS computes the self-certainty score; if it exceeds a learned threshold, the current best response is returned immediately. Otherwise, additional samples are drawn iteratively until certainty stabilizes or a maximum N is reached. Thresholds are calibrated per model and task domain using a small validation set. This creates a sequential, certainty-gated sampling procedure analogous to early-exit mechanisms but at the generation level. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended generation benchmarks (MT-Bench), comparing against fixed Best-of-N with self-certainty, uniform adaptive baselines, and reward-model-guided approaches. Metrics include accuracy vs. average samples per query (compute-accuracy Pareto curves), and we ablate threshold calibration strategies. We hypothesize SCGAS achieves equivalent accuracy to fixed Best-of-32 using 40-60% fewer total samples across mixed-difficulty datasets.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Iterative Refinement: Using Self-Certainty as a Signal for Targeted Self-Correction in LLMs
description:
Problem: While self-certainty effectively identifies high-quality responses via Best-of-N selection, low-certainty responses are simply discarded rather than improved. This wastes computation and ignores valuable information about *where* a response is uncertain, leaving a gap between selection-based and generation-based test-time compute scaling.

Proposed Method: We introduce Certainty-Guided Iterative Refinement (CGIR), which repurposes self-certainty scores not just for selection but as targeted refinement signals. First, we compute token-level and segment-level self-certainty by aggregating probability distributions across N samples. Low-certainty spans are identified as likely error sites. The model is then prompted to re-examine and revise specifically those low-certainty reasoning steps, conditioned on the high-certainty portions as anchors. This creates a hybrid approach: high-certainty responses are returned directly (Best-of-N), while low-certainty responses undergo certainty-guided revision passes before final selection.

Experiments: (1) Mathematical reasoning benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K) comparing CGIR against vanilla Best-of-N, self-consistency, and iterative self-correction baselines; (2) Analysis of refinement efficiency—accuracy gain per additional token generated; (3) Ablations on certainty thresholds for triggering refinement vs. direct selection; (4) Open-ended tasks (TruthfulQA, long-form QA) to test generalization. We hypothesize CGIR achieves better accuracy-compute tradeoffs than pure selection methods.

title: Adaptive Test-Time Computation Allocation via Self-Certainty Confidence Thresholds
description:
Problem: Best-of-N selection typically uses a fixed N across all queries, wasting computation on easy problems while potentially under-sampling difficult ones. An ideal system would dynamically allocate test-time compute based on query difficulty, stopping early when confident and sampling more when uncertain.

Proposed Method: We introduce Self-Certainty Adaptive Sampling (SCAS), which uses self-certainty scores as an online stopping criterion during Best-of-N generation. Rather than pre-committing to N samples, SCAS maintains a running self-certainty estimate after each new sample and stops generation when certainty exceeds a learned threshold or triggers a confidence plateau detector. We propose two variants: (1) a threshold-based approach where certainty thresholds are calibrated per-domain via held-out validation, and (2) a bandit-inspired approach that treats N-allocation as a sequential decision problem, maximizing accuracy subject to a compute budget constraint. We additionally train a lightweight meta-predictor that estimates required N from input complexity features before generation begins.

Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended tasks (TriviaQA, summarization). Metrics include accuracy-vs-FLOPs curves, average N consumed per query, and Pareto efficiency versus fixed-N baselines and reward model approaches. We demonstrate 30-50% compute reduction at matched accuracy compared to fixed N=16 or N=32 baselines.

title: Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding: Early Exit and Dynamic N Allocation for Efficient Test-Time Scaling
description:
Problem: Best-of-N selection with self-certainty still requires generating a fixed N samples per query regardless of problem difficulty, wasting computation on easy questions while potentially under-sampling hard ones. An adaptive mechanism that dynamically allocates compute based on real-time certainty signals would dramatically improve efficiency.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding (ASCT), which monitors the running self-certainty score after each generated sample and applies two mechanisms: (1) Early Exit — stop sampling once certainty exceeds a high-confidence threshold τ_high, indicating the model has converged on a reliable answer; (2) Extended Sampling — continue beyond the default N when certainty remains below τ_low, up to a maximum budget N_max. Thresholds are calibrated per model and task domain using a small validation set. We further propose a difficulty-aware budget predictor that estimates required N from the question embedding before generation begins, enabling batch-level compute planning.

Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended generation (AlpacaEval) comparing fixed-N self-certainty, reward model BoN, and ASCT. Key metrics include accuracy vs. average samples generated (compute-accuracy Pareto frontier), wall-clock time reduction, and calibration of certainty thresholds across difficulty strata. We expect 30-40% reduction in average samples while maintaining accuracy parity.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Distribution-Aware Best-of-N
description:

Second, we incorporate entropy-based diversity penalties that down-weight candidates when high certainty arises from degenerate repetition rather than genuine agreement. Third, we introduce a 'certainty gap' signal—the difference between the top-ranked and second-ranked candidate's self-certainty—as an abstention trigger when calibration uncertainty is high.

Experiments: (1) Calibration curves (ECE/ACE) comparing raw self-certainty vs. CSC across GSM8K, MATH, ARC, TruthfulQA, and medical QA benchmarks; (2) Abstention-accuracy tradeoff analysis; (3) Ablations isolating clustering granularity and diversity penalty weight; (4) Scaling behavior with N from 4 to 64; (5) Human evaluation on open-ended tasks where overconfidence is most pronounced.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Best-of-N Selection via Uncertainty Decomposition
description: Problem: Self-certainty selects responses by aggregating distributional confidence across N samples, but this signal can be systematically miscalibrated — models may exhibit high self-certainty for confidently wrong answers (epistemic overconfidence), particularly in out-of-distribution or ambiguous reasoning scenarios. title: Adaptive Sample Allocation via Self-Certainty Signals: Saving Test-Time Compute Through Early Stopping and Dynamic N Selection
description:
Problem: Best-of-N selection with fixed N wastes compute on easy queries (where early samples already yield high self-certainty) while potentially under-sampling hard queries. title: Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding: Dynamic Early-Exit in Best-of-N Selection
description:
Problem: Best-of-N selection with self-certainty still requires generating all N samples before selecting the best response, incurring unnecessary computation when high-certainty consensus emerges early. Current approaches treat N as a fixed hyperparameter rather than adapting it dynamically to query difficulty.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Self-Certainty (ASC), a sequential sampling framework that monitors self-certainty scores incrementally after each generated sample and exits early when certainty crosses a learned difficulty-conditioned threshold. Specifically, we train a lightweight calibration model that predicts the minimum samples needed for reliable selection given query characteristics (complexity indicators, initial token probabilities). During inference, ASC computes running self-certainty after each sample and terminates when the score exceeds the predicted threshold with high confidence, otherwise continuing up to N_max. We additionally propose a 'certainty plateau detector' that identifies when additional samples yield diminishing certainty gains.

Experiments: (1) Compare average samples-per-query and accuracy vs. fixed-N self-certainty on MATH, GSM8K, GPQA, and open-ended benchmarks; (2) Analyze compute-accuracy Pareto frontiers against reward model baselines; (3) Evaluate threshold calibration across model families (Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, Gemini); (4) Measure correlation between predicted difficulty and actual samples needed; (5) Ablate calibration model size and training data requirements.
