title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Uncertainty-Aware Best-of-N Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on certain reasoning patterns (e.g., familiar-looking but incorrect problems), causing self-certainty to select confidently wrong answers. This miscalibration undermines reliability in high-stakes domains like medical or mathematical reasoning.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty score with a lightweight calibration layer trained on a small held-out set to detect overconfidence regimes. CSC computes a disagreement-adjusted certainty score that penalizes cases where high token-level probability coexists with semantic diversity among top-N candidates (a signal of spurious confidence). We combine self-certainty with a contrastive signal: the KL divergence between the response distribution and a perturbed-prompt distribution, flagging outputs whose certainty is prompt-independent and thus potentially memorized rather than reasoned.

Experiments: (1) Calibration analysis across MATH, MedQA, and ARC-Challenge benchmarks measuring ECE before/after CSC; (2) Best-of-N accuracy comparisons against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward models at N∈{4,8,16,32,64}; (3) Ablation on the contrastive perturbation component; (4) Out-of-distribution generalization on GSM-Symbolic to test robustness to surface-level pattern matching. We expect CSC to close 40-60% of the accuracy gap between self-certainty and reward models on hard reasoning splits.

title: Calibrating Self-Certainty: When Distributional Confidence Misleads and How to Correct It
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes that higher aggregate token-probability distributions across N samples reliably signal response quality. However, this assumption may systematically fail in specific regimes: (1) when models are confidently wrong due to training distribution biases, (2) on tasks requiring rare or counter-intuitive reasoning steps where correct answers carry lower probability, and (3) when prompt phrasing artificially inflates certainty for incorrect responses. Understanding and correcting these failure modes is critical before deploying self-certainty at scale. Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the base self-certainty metric with a lightweight miscalibration detector. We first systematically characterize failure modes by constructing adversarial benchmark suites where self-certainty and correctness diverge. Then, we train a small probe (using only model internals—hidden states and attention patterns) to predict when self-certainty is miscalibrated, enabling selective fallback to more expensive reward models only in flagged cases. This creates an adaptive compute allocation strategy. Experiments: We evaluate on mathematical reasoning (MATH, GSM8K), factual QA (TriviaQA), and deliberately adversarial prompts. Metrics include calibration curves (ECE), selective prediction accuracy under compute budgets, and comparison against full reward-model baselines. We target 80% of reward-model accuracy at 30% of its computational cost.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Failures in Large Language Models
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on reasoning problems where they consistently generate plausible-but-wrong answers (e.g., math problems with common error patterns). This miscalibration undermines Best-of-N selection in precisely the cases where it matters most.

Method: We propose Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty score with a lightweight miscalibration detector. First, we train a small probe on held-out reasoning tasks that maps (self-certainty score, semantic diversity of N samples, answer distribution entropy) to a calibration correction factor. Second, when the probe detects high self-certainty despite detectable semantic diversity among wrong-looking candidates, CSC triggers a 'contrastive verification' step: generating targeted counter-arguments to the top candidate using the LLM itself, then reweighting scores based on argument-resistance. This avoids expensive reward models while correcting for systematic overconfidence.

Experiments: (1) Calibration analysis across MATH, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, and StrategyQA comparing self-certainty confidence vs. actual accuracy at varying N. (2) CSC vs. self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward-model baselines on accuracy and compute budget. (3) Ablation of probe features and contrastive verification contribution. (4) Scaling curves showing CSC maintains calibration as N increases where self-certainty degrades.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning in LLMs via Distributional Uncertainty Decomposition
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be confidently wrong—particularly on problems requiring multi-step reasoning where early errors propagate. This systematic overconfidence undermines Best-of-N selection in domains like mathematical proofs or medical diagnosis where confident errors are costly. Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into aleatoric uncertainty (inherent task ambiguity) and epistemic uncertainty (model knowledge gaps) by contrasting token-level probability distributions across semantically clustered response groups. When high self-certainty co-occurs with high inter-cluster disagreement, we flag responses as 'confidently inconsistent' and apply a lightweight correction step: prompting the model to explicitly verify its highest-certainty response against low-certainty alternatives. We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which reweights response scores by their cluster-conditional confidence, penalizing outlier-confident responses. Planned Experiments: (1) Benchmark on MATH, GSM8K, MedQA, and LegalBench comparing CSC vs. vanilla self-certainty, reward models, and self-consistency; (2) Calibration analysis via ECE and Brier scores across N={8,16,32,64}; (3) Ablation of decomposition components; (4) Human evaluation on open-ended medical reasoning where overconfidence has real consequences; (5) Scaling behavior across model sizes (7B–70B). Expected contribution: a training-free, reward-free method that matches reward model accuracy while avoiding confident failures.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Correcting Distributional Overconfidence in Best-of-N Selection via Temperature-Aware Normalization
description:
Problem: Self-certainty leverages token probability distributions to score LLM responses without external reward models, but raw token probabilities are known to be poorly calibrated—models exhibit systematic overconfidence in certain output styles, lengths, or formats, causing self-certainty scores to reflect surface-level distributional artifacts rather than true response quality. This miscalibration may cause Best-of-N selection to consistently favor verbose, repetitive, or stylistically familiar responses over correct but less probable ones.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which corrects for distributional biases by (1) applying length-normalized log-probability scoring to remove length bias, (2) learning a lightweight temperature-scaling correction per task domain using a small held-out validation set of N=50 examples, and (3) introducing a diversity-weighted aggregation that down-weights self-certainty scores when sampled responses cluster too narrowly in embedding space, preventing mode collapse in selection.

Experiments: We evaluate CSC across mathematical reasoning (MATH, GSM8K), code generation (HumanEval, MBPP), and open-ended QA (TriviaQA, ARC-Challenge) using Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 families. We measure: (1) selection accuracy vs. vanilla self-certainty and reward models at varying N, (2) calibration curves (ECE) of the scoring metric itself, (3) performance on intentionally length-biased prompt variants. We expect CSC to outperform vanilla self-certainty by 3-7% on mathematical tasks while maintaining efficiency advantages over reward models.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Chains via Uncertainty-Aware Best-of-N Selection
description:
Problem: Self-certainty leverages output probability distributions to select high-quality responses, but LLMs are known to be miscalibrated—exhibiting high distributional confidence even for incorrect reasoning chains, particularly on out-of-distribution problems. Second, we train a small calibration model (a shallow MLP) on held-out reasoning traces that maps (step-level certainty profile, answer entropy) → correctness probability, correcting systematic miscalibration without a full reward model. We compare against vanilla self-certainty, universal self-consistency, and ORMs across N∈{4,8,16,32,64}. Key metrics include accuracy, Expected Calibration Error, and performance degradation under distribution shift. Ablations isolate contributions of step-level decomposition, calibration, and diversity penalty.

description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on certain reasoning patterns (e.g., flawed but fluent chain-of-thought), causing self-certainty to consistently select wrong answers. This miscalibration is especially problematic in mathematical olympiad problems and multi-step logical reasoning where confident-sounding errors cluster together. title: Adaptive Sample Allocation for Best-of-N via Early Self-Certainty Estimation
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection improves LLM reasoning but wastes compute by generating all N samples before evaluation. description: Problem: Best-of-N selection typically applies a fixed N across all queries, wasting compute on easy problems while under-sampling difficult ones. title: Adaptive Best-of-N via Self-Certainty Thresholding: Knowing When to Stop Sampling

We augment this with a 'certainty-diversity tension' signal: when high self-certainty co-occurs with low semantic diversity across N samples (measured via embedding variance), we flag potential overconfidence and fall back to a hybrid scoring that incorporates token-level entropy patterns as a complementary signal. This requires no external reward model. Experiments: (1) Measure calibration error (ECE) of raw vs. calibrated self-certainty across MATH, MMLU-Pro, and MedQA; (2) Compare Best-of-N accuracy on adversarial benchmarks designed to elicit confident errors (ARC-Challenge variants, ambiguous reasoning); (3) Ablate the certainty-diversity tension threshold; (4) Evaluate computational overhead vs. reward model baselines at N=16,32,64.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Best-of-N Selection via Uncertainty Decomposition
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on certain input types (e.g., ambiguous questions, out-of-distribution topics, or adversarial prompts), causing Best-of-N selection to confidently pick wrong answers. This miscalibration undermines reliability in high-stakes applications. Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into aleatoric uncertainty (inherent task ambiguity, measured by entropy variance across N samples) and epistemic uncertainty (model knowledge gaps, measured by semantic clustering diversity). We introduce a calibrated self-certainty score that down-weights selections when epistemic uncertainty is high, and propose a fallback mechanism that triggers abstention or retrieval-augmented generation when both components exceed learned thresholds. Thresholds are calibrated using a small held-out validation set via temperature scaling adapted to the distributional certainty metric. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate calibration (ECE, reliability diagrams) on MMLU, TruthfulQA, and medical QA benchmarks comparing raw self-certainty vs. calibrated variant; (2) Adversarial stress tests with paraphrased misleading questions; (3) Ablations on fallback strategy effectiveness; (4) Scaling analysis across N={8,16,32,64} showing calibration holds as N grows; (5) Human evaluation on open-ended tasks where abstention is appropriate. Expected outcome: improved trustworthiness without sacrificing accuracy gains from Best-of-N.

title: Adaptive Best-of-N via Self-Certainty Thresholding: When to Stop Sampling
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection traditionally requires fixing N in advance, leading to wasted computation on easy queries (where N=1 suffices) and insufficient exploration on hard queries. Self-certainty provides a cheap quality signal, but its potential for adaptive early stopping remains unexplored. Proposed Method: We introduce Certainty-Adaptive Sampling (CAS), which dynamically determines the stopping point during Best-of-N generation. After each new sample, CAS computes a running self-certainty score across accumulated responses. Sampling halts when: (1) self-certainty exceeds a high-confidence threshold (easy query detected), or (2) self-certainty plateaus below a saturation threshold after a minimum number of samples (hard query—redirect to a fallback verifier). We additionally train a lightweight meta-predictor that maps per-query statistics (prompt complexity proxies, initial self-certainty trajectory) to optimal stopping thresholds, learned via offline regression on historical query-difficulty labels. Experiments: We evaluate CAS on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended instruction-following benchmarks (AlpacaEval). Metrics include accuracy-vs-FLOPs curves, average N used per difficulty quartile, and comparison against fixed-N self-certainty, fixed-N reward models, and speculative decoding baselines. We hypothesize CAS achieves competitive accuracy with 40-60% fewer samples on average, establishing a new Pareto frontier for test-time compute efficiency.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Best-of-N Selection via Epistemic Uncertainty Decomposition
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on hard or out-of-distribution problems, causing Best-of-N selection to confidently pick wrong answers. This miscalibration is especially dangerous in high-stakes domains like medical reasoning or formal mathematics where confident errors are worse than abstention. Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty scores into aleatoric uncertainty (inherent task ambiguity, estimated via response entropy across samples) and epistemic uncertainty (model knowledge gaps, estimated via disagreement between subsets of N samples using a jackknife-style resampling). We introduce a calibration layer that adjusts raw self-certainty scores based on the epistemic-to-aleatoric ratio, downweighting selections when epistemic uncertainty is disproportionately high. When calibrated certainty falls below a learned threshold, the system triggers a fallback: either abstention or targeted retrieval-augmented generation. Planned Experiments: (1) Calibration curves comparing raw vs. calibrated self-certainty across MATH, MedQA, and LiveCodeBench; (2) ECE and Brier score comparisons against reward model baselines; (3) Selective prediction experiments measuring accuracy-abstention tradeoffs; (4) Ablations on jackknife subset sizes; (5) Human evaluation on cases where calibrated self-certainty triggers abstention vs. confident wrong answers from vanilla self-certainty.

title: Adaptive Best-of-N Stopping via Self-Certainty Confidence Bounds
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection improves LLM reasoning but requires pre-specifying N, forcing a trade-off between quality and compute. Easy queries waste computation generating N samples while hard queries may benefit from N>>standard budgets. We need a principled early-stopping mechanism that allocates samples dynamically based on problem difficulty. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveCertainty, which treats self-certainty scores as a sequential estimation process. After each new sample, we compute a running self-certainty estimate and its variance across the current sample pool. We apply a sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) with confidence bounds derived from bootstrapped self-certainty distributions to decide whether to stop sampling or continue. When self-certainty converges above a learned threshold (calibrated per model/domain), we stop early; when certainty remains low after a minimum budget, we escalate to a larger N. The thresholds are learned on a small validation set without reward models. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare average samples-per-query vs. accuracy on MATH, GSM8K, GPQA, and open-ended TruthfulQA against fixed-N self-certainty and reward model baselines; (2) Measure compute-accuracy Pareto curves showing AdaptiveCertainty dominates fixed-N; (3) Ablate stopping thresholds and minimum/maximum N bounds; (4) Evaluate calibration across model families (Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3).

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Paths in LLMs via Distributional Uncertainty Decomposition
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes that higher distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can exhibit systematically overconfident distributions on incorrect reasoning chains—particularly for questions near their training distribution but outside their competence boundary. This 'confident-but-wrong' failure mode undermines Best-of-N selection reliability.

Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into two components: (1) aleatoric uncertainty, reflecting genuine ambiguity in the problem, and (2) epistemic uncertainty, reflecting model knowledge gaps. We estimate epistemic uncertainty by comparing self-certainty scores across layers of the model (using hidden-state entropy at intermediate transformer layers vs. final output distributions). Responses where final-layer certainty is high but intermediate-layer certainty is low are flagged as 'overconfident'—the model converged too quickly to an answer. We propose a calibrated self-certainty score that penalizes such overconfidence and re-ranks Best-of-N candidates accordingly, without any external reward model.

Experiments: We evaluate on MATH-500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and a new adversarial benchmark of 'confident mistakes' curated from model failure modes. We compare against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model baselines. We measure calibration (ECE), accuracy under Best-of-N selection, and specifically analyze performance on out-of-distribution reasoning problems where overconfidence is most prevalent.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Chains via Distributional Uncertainty Decomposition
description:
Problem: While self-certainty effectively identifies high-quality responses by aggregating distributional confidence across samples, it conflates two distinct phenomena: genuine model competence (aleatoric certainty) and spurious overconfidence from repetitive or degenerate outputs (epistemic miscalibration). A model that consistently generates confident but wrong reasoning chains will score highly under self-certainty despite being systematically incorrect, particularly in domains requiring multi-step arithmetic or symbolic reasoning.

Proposed Method: We decompose self-certainty into two components: (1) consensus certainty—agreement across semantically distinct reasoning paths, and (2) diversity penalty—a term that discounts certainty when sampled responses collapse onto near-identical surface forms. We use embedding-space clustering to detect semantic degeneracy and reweight individual sample contributions to the aggregate certainty score. Additionally, we propose a lightweight self-refinement trigger: when high certainty but low diversity is detected, the model is prompted to generate alternative reasoning chains via contrastive decoding.

Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, and a new adversarial benchmark of 'confident-but-wrong' problems. We compare against vanilla self-certainty, self-consistency, and reward model baselines, measuring accuracy, calibration error, and response diversity. Ablations isolate the contribution of diversity penalties versus refinement triggering across model scales (7B–70B).

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Paths in LLMs
description: Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can be systematically overconfident on certain reasoning patterns (e.g., common mathematical shortcuts, culturally prevalent answers), producing high self-certainty scores for wrong answers. This miscalibration undermines reliability in high-stakes domains like medical diagnosis or legal reasoning. Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments the self-certainty metric with a lightweight calibration layer trained on a small held-out validation set. Specifically, we (1) model the relationship between self-certainty scores and empirical accuracy using isotonic regression per task category, (2) identify 'certainty traps'—clusters of responses with high self-certainty but low accuracy—using contrastive decoding with perturbed prompts to expose overconfident failure modes, and (3) apply a confidence-penalized reranking that discounts self-certainty scores when response diversity is abnormally low (indicating mode collapse). Planned Experiments: We evaluate CSC on MATH, MedQA, LegalBench, and ARC-Challenge across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and Mistral families. We measure calibration error (ECE), accuracy-vs-N scaling curves, and compare against vanilla self-certainty, universal self-consistency, and reward model baselines. We specifically ablate performance on out-of-distribution prompts designed to trigger known LLM reasoning biases.

title: Adaptive Self-Certainty Thresholding: Early Exit and Dynamic N Allocation for Efficient Test-Time Scaling
description: Problem: Self-certainty improves Best-of-N selection without reward models, but current approaches use a fixed N for all queries regardless of difficulty—wasting computation on easy problems and under-sampling hard ones. We propose Adaptive Self-Certainty (ASC), a method that dynamically allocates the number of samples N per query by monitoring the self-certainty score as samples accumulate. Method: We treat self-certainty as a sequential signal. For each query, we generate samples incrementally and compute a running self-certainty estimate. If certainty exceeds a high threshold (confident answer found), we exit early; if it plateaus below a low threshold after some minimum N, we trigger a fallback (e.g., escalate to a larger model or reward model). A learned calibration layer maps raw self-certainty scores to calibrated confidence estimates using a small held-out set, enabling reliable threshold-setting across model families. Experiments: (1) Compare FLOPs vs. accuracy tradeoffs against fixed-N self-certainty, reward models, and self-consistency on MATH, GSM8K, GPQA, and open-ended creative tasks; (2) Analyze threshold sensitivity and calibration quality; (3) Measure wall-clock efficiency gains on a production-style serving simulator; (4) Evaluate the cascading fallback strategy. We expect 30–50% average compute reduction at matched accuracy.

title: Adaptive Sample Allocation via Self-Certainty Signals: Efficient Test-Time Compute Budgeting for LLMs
description: Problem: Best-of-N selection typically allocates a fixed N samples per query regardless of problem difficulty, wasting compute on easy queries while undersampling hard ones. Self-certainty provides a natural signal for difficulty estimation, but no principled framework exists for using it to dynamically allocate samples during inference. Proposed Method: We introduce Self-Certainty-Guided Adaptive Sampling (SCAS), a sequential test-time compute allocation strategy. Starting from a small initial pool (N=2), SCAS computes running self-certainty scores after each batch of samples. If certainty exceeds a high-confidence threshold, sampling halts early; if certainty remains low after a mid-point checkpoint, additional samples are drawn up to a budget cap. We further propose a meta-learned threshold calibration procedure that maps self-certainty trajectories to expected accuracy gains using a lightweight regression model trained on held-out query-response pairs. This enables query-adaptive budgeting without reward models. Experiments: We evaluate SCAS on MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and open-ended writing tasks across Llama-3, Mistral, and Qwen-2.5 model families. We measure accuracy-vs-FLOPs Pareto curves against fixed-N baselines, uniform adaptive compute methods, and reward-model-guided strategies, demonstrating that SCAS achieves comparable accuracy at 30-50% reduced average sample cost while maintaining scalability benefits.

title: Calibrated Self-Certainty: Detecting and Correcting Overconfident Reasoning Failures in LLMs
description:
Problem: Self-certainty assumes high distributional confidence correlates with correctness, but LLMs can exhibit systematic overconfidence on certain problem types (e.g., math problems requiring multi-step reasoning, counterfactual queries), producing confidently wrong answers that self-certainty would incorrectly select. This miscalibration represents a critical failure mode for deployment.

Proposed Method: We introduce Calibrated Self-Certainty (CSC), which augments self-certainty with a lightweight calibration layer. First, we characterize self-certainty miscalibration across problem taxonomies by constructing a 'confidence-correctness reliability diagram' per domain. Second, we train a small auxiliary probe (using only LLM-internal features: self-certainty score, response entropy, problem type embedding) to predict when self-certainty will be overconfident. When overconfidence is flagged, CSC triggers a targeted diversity-promoting resampling strategy that increases temperature selectively to escape false-confidence basins. Third, we apply isotonic regression calibration to self-certainty scores conditioned on problem type.

Experiments: (1) Measure miscalibration of vanilla self-certainty across MATH, GSM8K, ARC, TruthfulQA, and open-ended creative tasks; (2) Compare CSC vs. self-certainty, reward models, and process reward models on accuracy and Expected Calibration Error; (3) Ablate calibration components; (4) Test cross-model transfer of the calibration probe across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and Mistral families.
